details.recommendationText: To help the family, an inclusive approach focusing on both environmental improvements and social support is recommended. Strengthening on their community involvement, programs that provide livelihood opportunities that can help stabilize their income and improve their living conditions. Enhancing their awareness of health and safety, and encouraging greater participation in social protection programs, will empower them further. Regular monitoring and follow-up are essential to ensure the success and to adjust strategies as their needs change over time.

presentingProblem.html: The family is experiencing financial stress resulting to difficulty in providing the educational needs of their in-school child Art Haiden.

client.html:
Margie and Rodgen, 38- and 42-year-olds live in Barangay Basiao, Pres. Carlos P. Garcia, Bohol. Rodgen is a fisherman while Margie is a fish vendor. She sells Rodgen’s catch. Art Haiden is Margie’s son from her previous partner and he is bringing Margie’s maiden name. Margie and Rodgen have been married for 5 years. The couple are both high school graduates; they can read and write. Art Haide is currently in Grade 12.
Margie appears to be participative in Family Development Sessions; she demonstrated pro-activeness during the sessions and often shares to the group. She is a member of SLPA and volunteers in KALAHI projects.
The family was identified as poor in Listahahan last 2019 and was registered in set 12A last March 2023. They have been active partner-beneficiaries in the program for 3 years.

socioEconomic.html:
They are living in their ancestral house located in the remote part of the barangay. It is made of light materials, has one room and a comfort room located outside their house. The house appears to be clean, simple and modest.
Margie expressed that even though they live simply, they work together to keep their home running smoothly. Everyone in the family assumes household chores. Margie oversees the household chores. Whenever she is out selling fish, Art Haiden takes care of the chores – particularly cooking. Sometimes he helps Margie in selling small goods to earn extra money.
They don’t often go to church but Margie said her family remains hopeful for a better future especially for Art Haiden. She said, they dream of better living conditions and more opportunities to improve their income.

healthCondition.html: The family appears to be healthy. They have not experienced any serious medical illness. Margie said they are able to avail barangay health services within the past six months. The family has a segregated garbage bin. They also own a water-sealed comfort room. There is no sign of mental health issues nor gender-based issues in the family. Margie said that when there are coming typhoons, Rodgen does not go out fishing and the family seeks safety through staying in the nearby school  which is the designated evacuation center.

environmentalLivingConditions.html:
The family lives a 15-minute motorcycle ride from the barangay center. Their only water source is a shared deep well. Some families can afford to have their own deep well, but since Margie’s relatives own the well near them, they can access the water for free. For drinking water, they buy from refilling stations in their barangay at Php25 per gallon. The community promotes waste segregation, with plastic waste collected by the local government unit (LGU), and they prohibit burning trash in each home. They have electricity, which provides power to light up the entire barangay.
The family has not experienced conflicts in their neighborhood.

environmentCommunity.html: The community is 7.2 kilometers from the town center. It takes about 20 minutes to travel there by motor vehicle. People can reach the community by riding a public jeep or motorbike along San Vicente-Villa Milagrosa Road. Most houses are near the shore, while some are near the mountain. The main jobs of the residents are fishing and farming. The barangay has basic facilities, including an emergency rescue vehicle, a health station, a small gymnasium, a chapel, an elementary ofschool, a high school, and a Day Center. These are all located near the Barangay Hall. The health center has a Barangay Health Worker on duty every day. There is also a visiting midwife or nurse who provides health check-ups, vaccinations, and other health services. Water comes mainly from deep wells. There are several communal wells, and some households have their own for laundry and cooking. The barangay has a water refilling station along the road, which residents can access for drinking water, with door-to-door delivery available. Most households have electricity. The residents practice waste segregation and proper waste disposal. Some burn biodegradable wastes. Every two to three months, the local government staff collect and buy plastic waste, working with the barangay council. Residents gather their plastic garbage and bring it to the collection point. Most homes have a water-sealed toilet. The community is quiet and safe. During a disaster, residents living near the shore are advised to evacuate to the elementary or high school, which serve as evacuation sites for the barangay.

caseAssessment.html:
The Acuesta family was checked using the Family Risk and Vulnerability Assessment (FRVA). The results showed they have low risk in finances and the environment, and no risks in health, safety, or protecting children.

Their latest Social Welfare and Development Indicator (SWDI) assessment was done on August 3, 2025. It showed their family’s income is at Level 2, meaning they just meet basic needs (subsistence level). Their average monthly income per person is Php2,938.88. The poverty line in Bohol is Php2,170.74 per person each month, and the average food cost in the province is Php1,515.83.

The family has this year to be in the program since they will be ineligible for the program due to Art Haiden’s graduation in Senior High School.

The family head's seasonal income is insufficient to cover all the growing educational expenses of their son, Art. Their meager earnings are just enough to meet basic needs, with an average monthly income per person of Php2,938.88, which is slightly above the poverty line but still insufficient to comfortably afford health and educational expenses. The rising health and education costs have put a real strain on their finances. In addition, living on a remote island and relying only on fishing, which can easily be affected by weather and environmental conditions, poses a burden in terms of the family's finances. The Acuesta family have been struggling for a while but this burden was unloaded through the aid of the program, but things are getting more pressing now that Art Haiden is almost done with school and they will soon not be able to get some financial help from the government making him difficult to pursue on his tertiary education.

The family’s situation is not entirely permanent. The family may have big problems which mainly come from social and economic issues that can be solved with the right help, support, and community programs. Acuesta’s family shows resiliency amidst their financial difficulties. They're involved in their community, which shows they want to change and improve for their family. Margie, in particular, has demonstrated her hardworking nature and willingness to seek solutions, which suggests that with appropriate support given, positive change is achievable.

Their environment also offers some available resources that can promote improvement. Local government programs that facilitate waste management, health services, and possible livelihood initiatives. The community also has basic facilities such as a health station, barangay hall, and water refilling stations, which can support health and sanitation needs. However, restraining forces such as limited income, geographic location, and dependence on vulnerable livelihood sources poses significant barriers to the family’s progress. These factors can make it hard to find stable jobs and get the services they need. Though the family’s problem is not immediately life-threatening, the on-going financial difficulties affect their ability to access necessary health and educational services, which are critical for their long-term well-being. Addressing these issues immediately is important to prevent further threat to their level of well-being.

In the theory of Maslow's Hierarchy of needs emphasizes that people worry about food, housing, and feeling safe before they can think about things like school or personal growth. The Acuesta family is struggling because they don't have much money, so it's hard for them to regularly meet these basic needs. This affects how happy and healthy they are, and how they develop as people. But despite being financially incapable the Acuesta family was able to send Art Haiden to school through the help of the program nearing its completion in Senior High School education.

The Family Systems Theory looks at the Acuesta family as a group where everyone affects everyone else. Because they're having financial difficulties, it changes how they interact, their relationships, and how they handle tough times together. If we understand how they're all connected, we can create support programs that help the whole family. The Acuesta family’s strategies in overcoming struggles are done through collaborative and proactive approach. They involve everyone in seeking solutions to their problems which make them a functional family and could be a good asset to the family in attaining improved level of well-being.

The Ecological Systems Theory, developed by Bronfenbrenner, says that things like community programs, government help, and where the family lives are important. The Acuesta family lives far away from many things, being in a remote area, and it's hard for them to get services easily when needed. This has a big impact on their financial situation. Despite these struggles, the Acuesta family is strong and connected to their community. These are good things that can help them make their lives better. The family is good at expressing for themselves, and their involvement in community groups are strengths that help them. They know where to access resources according to their needs.

Lastly, Amartya Sen's Capability Approach is all about giving people and families the tools they need to live fulfilling lives. By boosting Acuesta’s income through giving livelihood capital assistance or any possible livelihood opportunities, making sure their child, Art Haiden can get to school, and providing health services, it can open up new doors for them and become better in individual functions and their overall well-being. Looking at this, through the lens of what shapes people’s condition and how to fight poverty, it's clear that acting presently is crucial. The program aims to break the intergenerational cycle of poverty and make sure that families have a brighter future ahead of them through investing in education, healthcare, and economic opportunities so that poo families will have an equal opportunity to have a better life. Poverty is a multifaceted issue, and early action is key to making a real difference in people's lives. For instance, if children have access to good schools and healthcare from a young age, they're more likely to stay healthy, get a good education, and find better jobs in the future. This not only improves their lives but also benefits their families and communities. When families have enough money, good health, and access to education, they're better positioned to take advantage of opportunities and make choices that align with their values and dreams. And when communities invest in programs and policies that support families, they're creating a ripple effect that can lead to sustainable and positive change.
